initial_observation.encounter_context: sought our clinic’s assistance in November 2020 after experiencing persistent symptoms
initial_observation.chief_complaint: left-sided pulsatile tinnitus (PT) for the past 10 months
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: The patient had persistent left-sided PT despite multiple prior misdiagnoses including migraine and subjective tinnitus, previously seen at tertiary hospitals ENT departments. PT was slightly reduced with strong compression of the internal carotid artery but not affected by internal jugular vein compression. No ocular symptoms or abnormalities on ocular assessments and physical exam. CT and MR scans showed no temporal bone dehiscence but revealed a small hyperintense signal region in the lesser sphenoid wing and left para-cavernous sinus regions indicative of dural arteriovenous fistula. The patient declined invasive diagnostics and elected conservative follow-up.

evidence_items.source_text: A 31-year-old female patient, who had been experiencing left-sided PT for the past 10 months, sought our clinic’s assistance in November 2020.

Ocular assessments, such as fundoscopy, visual field examination, and orbital ultrasound, uncovered no irregularities. A physical examination did not reveal any signs of heightened conjunctival vascularity, exophthalmia, oculomotor paralysis, or visual acuity loss.
CT showed no signs of temporal bone dehiscence at either the sigmoid plate or the jugular bulb regions.

The three-dimensional time-of-flight (TOF) MR angiography showed a relatively small region of hyperintense signal at the lesser SW region and the left para-CS (laterocavernous sinus) region (Figure 1), which extends to its efferent outlets, typically the SOV and inferior ophthalmic vein (IOV), and through the meningeal emissary veins to the pterygoid plexus (Figure 2).

Upon this discovery, the subject was referred to interventional radiology/neurology. However, due to the patient’s unwillingness to undergo surgical intervention or digital subtraction angiography (DSA) examination, the subject chose conservative observation and took no medication, but was kept under follow-up care.
The subject’s PT abruptly ceased without any apparent provocation after persisting for a total duration of 30 months. The tinnitus handicap inventory score decreased from 32 to 0.
A subsequent 3D-TOF MR angiography follow-up examination failed to detect any residual high-intensity signals within the SW region, para-CS, or any of the associated efferent vessels.
Furthermore, the subject did not report experiencing any ocular symptoms or adverse effects subsequent to the cessation of PT.
A follow-up MR angiography was conducted 42 months after the initial PT onset, revealing no signs of PT recurrence and no radiologic indications of DAVF (Figure 1).

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: This study presents a unique case of Cognard IIa SW-SOV DAVF with PT as the sole symptom and a rare incidence of the spontaneous closure of the fistula.
accepted_aliases: Sphenoid wing (SW) dural arteriovenous fistula (DAVF) draining into superior ophthalmic vein (SOV)
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: The three-dimensional time-of-flight (TOF) MR angiography showed a relatively small region of hyperintense signal at the lesser SW region and the left para-CS (laterocavernous sinus) region (Figure 1), which extends to its efferent outlets, typically the SOV and inferior ophthalmic vein (IOV), and through the meningeal emissary veins to the pterygoid plexus (Figure 2).

While up to 70% of transverse-sigmoid sinus DAVFs have been reported to have PT, PT as a standalone symptom in DAVF patients comprises only approximately 10%. Notably, PT has been reported in 35.7 ~ 41% of SW-SOV-associated DAVFs, most of which are often accompanied by proptosis, chemosis, and other neurologic deficits. To date, there have been no reports of PT as the sole symptom of SW-SOV DAVFs.

Ocular assessments, such as fundoscopy, visual field examination, and orbital ultrasound, uncovered no irregularities. A physical examination did not reveal any signs of heightened conjunctival vascularity, exophthalmia, oculomotor paralysis, or visual acuity loss.

The subject’s PT abruptly ceased without any apparent provocation after persisting for a total duration of 30 months. The tinnitus handicap inventory score decreased from 32 to 0. A subsequent 3D-TOF MR angiography follow-up examination failed to detect any residual high-intensity signals within the SW region, para-CS, or any of the associated efferent vessels.

This case study serves to underscore the occurrence of PT associated with DAVF in the SW and orbital regions, even in the absence of discernible hyperintense signals on MR angiogram screenings focusing on pathologies proximate to the auditory apparatus.
